overall_assessment.realism: The samples are highly realistic, reflecting common business email compromise scenarios with detailed and plausible email headers, authentication results, SMTP logs, domain registration data, and behavioral anomalies. The inclusion of specific sender IPs, geolocations, email volumes, and authentication failures aligns well with real-world attack patterns. The email bodies and subjects are contextually appropriate and consistent with typical social engineering tactics used in BEC attacks.
overall_assessment.consistency: The dataset is consistent and adheres well to a uniform schema across all samples. Each entry contains the same top-level keys and nested structures, including scenario descriptions, technical data with subfields (email headers, body, SMTP logs, domain registration, email authentication, unusual sending patterns), indicators, detection methods, and relevant MITRE techniques. The formatting of timestamps, IP addresses, and domain information is consistent. Minor variations in email client versions and timestamps are realistic and do not break schema uniformity.
suggestions: Include explicit multi-factor authentication (MFA) status or mention in the technical data to highlight whether MFA was bypassed or absent, as this is critical in BEC scenarios.
Add more diversity in sender IP geolocations and timestamps to cover a broader range of anomaly detection cases, including weekends or holidays.
Incorporate examples with successful SPF/DKIM passes but suspicious behavioral indicators to represent more sophisticated attacks.
Standardize the representation of email body placeholders in SMTP transaction logs (e.g., consistently use '[Email body]' or '[Email body content]') for clarity.
Consider adding a field for email client user-agent strings parsed into structured data to facilitate automated analysis.
Include explicit mention of whether the domain registration details are consistent with the sender's claimed organization to enhance detection context.
Add examples where DMARC policy is set to 'reject' but spoofed emails still appear, to illustrate enforcement gaps or misconfigurations.
